question: The Treaty of Lausanne exempted the Greeks of Imbros and Tenedos from the Greece-Türkiye population exchange, providing for extensive autonomy, a condition which has still today never been implemented. In violation of Articles 14 and 37-44 of Part III of the Treaty, Türkiye revoked all the rights of the residents of Imbros and Tenedos, and banned the teaching of the Greek language.
The existence of local police, controlled by the Greek minority, was never implemented, and the population of the islands was altered due to extensive settlements from the depths of Türkiye.

Greek properties were lost, estates and forest lands were forcibly expropriated, churches and schools were closed, and the export of livestock products and the possession of watercraft were prohibited, with the result that fishing was also affected. At the same time, there was an organised/instigated practice of anti-Greek violence, so that eventually the Imbrians and Tenedians fled to Greece and elsewhere.

Today, Imbros and Tenedos have a fraction of the Greek population who were living there when the Lausanne Treaty was signed. Imbros and Tenedos were an obvious example (case study) of absolute ethnic cleansing of the population. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Given that the Treaty was co-signed by Greece, Türkiye, Italy, France and Romania, among other countries, is it bound by the Treaty of Lausanne, and does it wish for it to be observed?

Has it ever raised, or does it intend to raise, the issue of the return of confiscated property to the descendants of the evicted inhabitants of the islands? If not, what procedure is required in order to do so?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.2.2024) The EU has repeatedly expressed its expectation from Türkiye to unequivocally commit itself to good neighbourly relations, international agreements and the peaceful settlement of disputes, in accordance with the United Nations Charter, having recourse, if necessary, to the International Court of Justice1.

Last year marked the centennial from the signature of the Treaty of Lausanne. It is encouraging that 2023 saw a positive development of Greek-Turkish relations, culminating, in December, with a meeting at the highest level. Regarding in particular property rights, the Commission has continuously reflected issues in this regard in its annual country reports, most recently in the 2023 Türkiye Report2 .

The report clearly mentions the Council of Europe Resolution 1625 of 20083 regarding property rights on the islands of Gökçeada (Imbros) and Bozcaada (Tenedos) that still need to be fully implemented.

The report also emphasizes that there is an urgent need to revise the relevant legislation on the issue of property rights for non-Muslim minorities and other legislation covering all issues of property rights to ensure a more comprehensive framework. The EU will continue monitoring these aspects, adequately raising them in the institutional documents.
